segments.text: Right now, somewhere in the ocean, about a hundred people are asleep inside a steel tube,
hundreds of meters below the surface. On every thumbnail of that hull,
the sea is pressing down with roughly the weight of a grown adult.
If one hole the size of a coin opened up, water would come through faster than a racing car.
And if it did, nobody would be coming to help, because nobody knows where that tube is.
That last part is not a flaw, it is the design. So here is the question.
A submarine has to sink on purpose, then come back up. It has to carry people who need to breathe,
drive a machine that normally needs air, and stay silent in a medium where sound carries for
commonitors. How does one vessel do all of that? The answer comes as a chain. Each system on a
submarine exists because the one before it solved a problem and created a new one. Start with the
first problem, the sea itself. Pressure rises by about one atmosphere for every 10 meters of depth,
so at 400 meters a hull is carrying around 40 times the pressure at the surface. That is why submarine
hulls are cylinders with rounded ends, which spread the load evenly, and why they are built from thick
steel ribbed with frames inside. The exact depth a modern boat can reach is secret, and the figures
that circulate are guesses. What is known is that there are two numbers. There is a test depth,
which the boat is certified to reach, and a deeper crush depth, which nobody wants to discover. A hull that
strong is also very heavy, and now the flaw shows up. A sealed steel tube floats, because it is full of
air. To go under, a submarine has to make itself heavier than the water it pushes aside, and to come
back, lighter. It does this with ballast tanks. To dive, it opens vents at the top of the tanks and lets
seawater flood in while the air escapes. To surface, it blows compressed air into the tanks and pushes the
water out. Notice how simple that is. A submarine is a ship that goes down by being filled, and up by being
emptied. Diving is only the easy half. The hard half is stopping at the right depth, because a submarine that is
almost exactly as heavy as the water around it is almost impossible to leave alone. Seawater gets denser as it
gets colder and saltier, so the boat is lighter in one layer and heavier in the next. The crew eats, and the boat gets lighter.
A torpedo weighing over a ton and a half leaves the tube, and the boat suddenly rises, so water has to
rush into a compensating tank in the same moment, or the submarine would break the surface in the
middle of an attack. Small trim tanks inside the hull do this constant balancing, and the rule is that
no change in weight goes uncorrected. Next comes steering, and here the submarine behaves like an
aircraft more than a ship. It has horizontal planes, near the bow or on the sail, that tilt the boat up or
down as water flows over them, and a rudder for turning. At speed, a few degrees of plane angle
moves the boat vertically. At slow speed, planes lose their bite, and the trim tanks have to do
the work. That detail will matter later, because slow is where a submarine wants to be. All of this
assumes the boat is moving, and moving takes an engine, and now the real trouble starts. A diesel
engine burns air, and below the surface there is none. The first answer was to run two systems. On the
surface, the diesels drive the boat, and charge a huge bank of batteries. Underwater, the electric
motors run from those batteries. It works, but the numbers are harsh. A diesel-electric submarine
going flat out can drain its batteries in around an hour, while creeping along at a few knots it can
last for days. So it spends most of its time slow, and every so often has to come up to a depth near
the surface and raise a snorkel, a tube that breathes air for the diesels. During those hours,
it is at its most exposed, a noisy engine and a little mast poking through the waves.
There are two ways out of that corner. One is air-independent propulsion, such as fuel cells
or small sterling engines, which let a conventional boat stay under for weeks at low speed without
snorkeling. The other is the reactor. A nuclear submarine makes steam from the heat of a reactor,
turns turbines with it, and needs no air at all. It can go fast, stay deep, and stay down for as long
as the people on board can stand it. Modern reactor cores are designed to last for decades
without refueling, which means the real limit on how long a nuclear submarine can stay submerged
is the pantry. Many navies plan patrols around the amount of food that can be loaded, which is a
strange thing to say about a machine that can split atoms. The reactor has one cost of its own.
Its coolant pumps can never be switched off, so a nuclear boat is never fully silent the way a
battery boat creeping along can be. The crew has the same dependence on air as the engine did,
and a boat that never surfaces has to manufacture its own. Oxygen comes mainly from electrolysis,
which splits seawater into oxygen and hydrogen, with the hydrogen sent overboard. The carbon dioxide
people breathe out is pulled from the air by scrubbers, a chemical process that runs continuously.
Fresh water is distilled from the sea. If any of that stops, the crew has hours, not days,
days, so it is the one set of systems with several backups. Now the boat can dive, hold depth, move,
and keep its people alive. And here is the problem that shapes everything else, because none of it is
any use if the enemy can hear it coming. Sound travels about four and a half times faster in water
than in air, and it can carry for many kilometers. Every pump, gear, and propeller blade is a voice,
so the quiet is built in. Machinery sits on rubber mounts and floating rafts,
so vibration never reaches the hull. Propellers are shaped with extreme care,
because bubbles forming on the blades at speed make a sharp recognizable crackle.
Hulls are covered with rubber tiles that soak up the sonar pulses sent at them. The effect is to
turn a hundred meter piece of machinery into something quieter than the ocean around it.
There is a nice irony in this. The same sea pressure that threatens the hull also helps in
one respect, because deeper water suppresses the bubbles on the propeller, so a boat can go faster
before it gets noisy. Going deeper really can make a submarine quieter. And since speed is the main
source of noise anyway, the most useful tactic a submarine has is simply to go slow, so the fastest
warship in the water mostly spends its life at the pace of a brisk walk. All that silence has a price,
which is blindness. Light fades within a few hundred meters, and radar does not work underwater. The only
real sense is sonar, and that comes in two forms. Active sonar sends a pulse and listens for the echo,
which tells you exactly where something is, and also tells everyone for comolitors exactly where you
are. Passive sonar just listens. A submarine commander who pings is a person who has decided
they would like to be found. So most boats listen almost all the time, using hull-mounted arrays and
a long cable of hydrophones towed behind them, and the ocean adds its own twists. Layers of different
temperature bend sound, so an enemy can sit just a few comolitors away and be for a while inaudible.
That brings the whole chain to its purpose, the weapon. A submarine carries torpedoes that can sink
ships and other submarines, and many carry cruise missiles fired from the same tubes or from vertical
launch cells. A few carry ballistic missiles, and for those boats the whole point is never to be found.
Their purpose is that someone, somewhere, knows there is one out there and cannot know where.
The measure of a good patrol is that nothing happened, and a crew can spend three months doing
the most difficult job in the Navy only to be told that the result was that no one noticed.
Which brings us to what films get wrong. In the movies, submarines ping constantly,
and the tension comes from the sound of a pulse bouncing off the hull. In practice,
whoever pings loses, and the contest is decided by who hears the other first. That is my own reading,
not a rule from a manual, but it suggests that a submarine's most valuable component is not its weapon
at all, it is its ears, and the quietness that keeps those ears working. So return to the tube full
of sleeping people. Every system in it, the hull, the tanks, the planes, the reactor, the scrubbers,
and the rubber tiles, answers the same short sentence, which is, stay down and make no sound.
Everything else is a patch for the problem that sentence creates.
